title: One Recipe, Three New Flavours
key_insight: A matrix is a tidy wall of mixing knobs: each row turns the same inputs into one new result.
body:
## A Wall of Mixing Knobs

You need three drinks from the same two ingredients. Instead of six loose knobs, put them in a tidy grid: each row is one drink recipe. That grid is a matrix.

Feed in the ingredient amounts, and every row mixes them into one result. The at-sign in Python tells the whole grid to do those multiply-and-add jobs together.

Neural networks use the same idea: one grid of learned knobs mixes incoming numbers into new numbers for the next layer.
common_mistakes: Thinking a matrix is only a table for storing data — in ML it often acts as a set of mixing instructions.
Using `*` when you mean matrix multiplication — `*` multiplies matching positions, while `@` combines rows with inputs.
Reading shape backwards — `(3, 2)` means three rows and two columns.
mini_exercise: Change the sweet-drink row from `[0.8, 0.2]` to `[0.5, 0.5]`. Predict the new first output before running the code, then check it.
real_world_usage: A small image classifier can treat each row of a weight matrix as one learned recipe for detecting a pattern. The inputs may be pixel features rather than ingredients, but the multiply-and-add operation is the same.
explain_back_prompt: Using the drink-machine story, explain what a matrix row means and why the number of columns must match the number of inputs.
